title: Adal Sultanate
capsule: The Adal Sultanate was founded around 1415 by Sabr ad-Din III on the Harar plateau after the fall of the Sultanate of Ifat, with its Walashma dynasty rulers making Dakkar, and later Harar and Aussa, their successive capitals. Real power increasingly shifted from the sultans to powerful emirs, most consequentially Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (known as Gragn, "the Left-Handed"), whose forces — equipped with Ottoman firearms — conquered roughly two-thirds of Christian Abyssinia between 1529 and 1543, prompting a Portuguese expeditionary force under Cristóvão da Gama to intervene on Abyssinia's behalf. Ahmad al-Ghazi was killed at the Battle of Wayna Daga in February 1543, shattering Adal's military supremacy. Oromo migrations into the Horn from the south then devastated Adal's hinterland, and by 1577 the capital was relocated to Aussa and the Imamate of Aussa proclaimed, effectively ending the sultanate as a coherent state.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The sultanate's core zones in the Ogaden and around Harar are documented in Abyssinian and Arabic sources, but peripheral boundaries — especially during Ahmad al-Ghazi's conquests — are expansive estimates derived from campaign narratives rather than fixed administrative lines.
